how-to-improve-concentration-in-children:
Concentration is not something a child can produce because they have been asked to. It rests on a set of capacities that mature over years, and a child who cannot hold attention on a Tuesday afternoon is usually short of one of them rather than short of willingness. Knowing which one changes what actually helps.

What concentration is made of

The single word covers at least four separate abilities, and they develop at different rates.

  • Holding a goal in mind. Keeping hold of what you are meant to be doing while doing it. This is working memory, and it is small in young children and grows into adolescence.
  • Ignoring what else is happening. Filtering out the sibling, the window, the itchy label. This is inhibition, and it is one of the slowest-maturing capacities there is.
  • Coming back after a break. Noticing that you have drifted and returning. Adults do this constantly and barely notice; children have to learn it.
  • Tolerating the boring bit. Nearly every worthwhile task has a stretch in the middle that is dull. Staying with it is partly attention and partly frustration tolerance.

The visible part of concentration is the last part to arrive. Judging a seven-year-old by it is like judging a building by the paint.

Rule out the ordinary explanations first

Before treating concentration as the problem, four things account for most of it in most households.

  • Sleep. The largest single variable, and consistently underestimated. A child an hour short across a week looks inattentive, not tired. Short sleep in children presents as fidgety and scattered far more often than as sleepy.
  • Difficulty. A task slightly beyond a child's current level produces avoidance that looks exactly like inattention. Watch what happens when the same child is given something they can do.
  • Interest. Attention is not a general tank. The child who cannot sit for ten minutes of handwriting and will sit for forty minutes of Lego does not have an attention deficit; they have a task problem.
  • The room. Television audible from the table, a sibling in view, a phone face-up. Adults filter these; a nine-year-old's filter is a fraction as strong.

What genuinely builds it

  • Protect uninterrupted stretches. A child deep in something should be left in it. Every interruption costs the return, and children who are constantly redirected never practise the long middle of a task.
  • Shorten the task, not the standard. Ten minutes finished well beats twenty-five abandoned. Length can rise as the capacity does.
  • One instruction at a time. Loading working memory with four steps guarantees a failure that gets read as not concentrating.
  • Physical movement first. Children generally settle better to a demanding task after movement than before it.
  • Games that load the capacities directly. Anything requiring you to hold a rule and inhibit a response. Simon Says, card games with changing rules, memory games. These are not enrichment; they are the specific muscles.
  • Reduce the background. A cleared table and a closed door outperform every technique in this list.

What does not help

Telling a child to concentrate. Longer sessions on the theory that stamina is built by endurance. Rewards for finishing, which shift the focus to the reward and away from the task. And commercial brain-training programmes, whose gains have repeatedly been shown to appear on the trained task and not to transfer to schoolwork or daily life.

When to ask somebody

If the difficulty is present across settings, home and school both, has lasted more than six months, and is genuinely interfering with learning or friendships, it is worth raising with somebody who can observe your child directly. Early support is lighter than later support, and asking costs nothing.

Concentration is not extracted from a child on command. It is built by the conditions around them and by capacities that arrive on their own schedule.

This piece is general guidance and is not a substitute for an assessment by someone who knows your child.
why-cant-my-child-focus:
Before concluding that a child has a focus problem, it is worth being systematic about four ordinary explanations. In most households one of them is the answer, and the fourth, the one about the task itself, is the one parents reach for last.

One: they are not sleeping enough

This is the biggest single factor and the least suspected, because short sleep in children does not look like tiredness. It looks like fidgeting, silliness, irritability and an inability to settle, which reads as behaviour rather than as a physiological state.

An hour short each night across a school week is enough to change a child noticeably. Before anything else, count the hours honestly against what is typical for the age, and look at how long it actually takes them to fall asleep rather than what time they went up.

Two: the work is too hard

A task slightly beyond a child's current level produces avoidance, wriggling, sharpening pencils, sudden urgent needs. Behaviour indistinguishable from inattention. The child is not failing to concentrate; they are managing the discomfort of not being able to do it.

The check is straightforward: give the same child something comfortably within reach and watch. If focus appears immediately, the problem is difficulty, and the answer is to adjust the work rather than the child.

Attention is not a general tank a child either has or lacks. It is largely a function of what they have been asked to attend to.

Three: it does not interest them

Every parent has noticed the contradiction. No attention for handwriting, unbroken attention for a construction set. This is not hypocrisy on the child's part and it does not mean they could focus on handwriting if they wanted to badly enough.

Interest genuinely changes the amount of attention available. That is true of adults too; we are simply better at forcing ourselves. A child's capacity to override low interest is one of the last things to mature, so a mismatch between task and interest shows up far more starkly.

Four: the room is working against them

Adults filter background so automatically that we underestimate how weak a child's filter is. A television audible two rooms away, a sibling in the line of sight, a phone face-up on the table. Each is a demand on the exact capacity the task needs.

Clearing the surface, closing the door and removing the screen from view does more for most children than any technique.

Working through it

Change one thing for a fortnight, not four things for a week. Most families find their answer in sleep or in difficulty, and both take a couple of weeks to show.

Keep a rough note of when focus is worst. If it is always the same time of day, that points at tiredness or hunger. If it is always the same subject, that points at difficulty. If it is genuinely everywhere and always, that is the pattern worth taking further.

When to ask for a proper look

Across settings, for more than six months, and getting in the way of learning or friendships. Those three together are the threshold worth acting on, not one difficult term, and not a comparison with a sibling.

Start with sleep. It is the least interesting answer and it is right more often than any of the others.

This piece is general guidance and is not a substitute for an assessment by someone who knows your child.
attention-span-by-age-what-is-normal:
There is a widely circulated rule that a child can attend for two to five minutes per year of age. It appears in school newsletters, parenting books and a great many articles. It has no solid research base, and it is worth knowing that before measuring your child against it.

Why a single number cannot be right

Attention is not one capacity with one duration. The same six-year-old will hold a construction task for forty minutes, a picture book for fifteen, a handwriting sheet for six, and a spoken instruction for about four seconds. All four are that child's real attention span.

What changes the number is not the child but the task, and specifically four things about it: how interesting it is, how difficult it is, whether it is self-directed or imposed, and whether the child chose to start.

Any figure that does not name the task is describing nothing.

What can reasonably be said

Broad, heavily caveated observations rather than a table:

  • Two to four. A few minutes on an imposed task; much longer on absorbing self-chosen play. Sustained attention to an adult's agenda is barely present, and should not be expected.
  • Four to six. Roughly ten to fifteen minutes of guided group activity in good conditions. Free play can run far longer.
  • Six to eight. Around fifteen to twenty minutes on structured work before a break helps. Rising noticeably across the two years.
  • Eight to eleven. Twenty to thirty minutes is realistic for work they can do; considerably less for work that is too hard.
  • Eleven and up. Approaching adult ranges on paper, but sharply reduced by tiredness, phones and social preoccupation, which are the real limiting factors at this age.

Treat all of these as "in reasonable conditions, on something within reach". None describes a child at four in the afternoon on short sleep.

The screen question

Parents often observe that their child will watch or play for hours and conclude the attention exists but is being withheld. It is worth being precise here. Screen media is designed to hold attention with constant novelty and immediate feedback, so it makes very few demands on the capacities that schoolwork needs. Sustaining a goal, ignoring distraction, tolerating a dull middle. Long screen engagement is genuine engagement; it is not evidence of the attention that reading a chapter requires.

Whether heavy screen use reduces attention over time is genuinely contested. The honest summary is that the associations are real but modest, the direction of causation is unclear, inattentive children may seek out screens, and the strong claims in both directions are ahead of the evidence.

What to do with all this

Stop measuring against a number. Watch your own child across a week and note where the attention is longest and where it collapses. That pattern is far more useful than any age chart, because it tells you which conditions produce focus in this particular child, and those conditions are the thing you can change.

If a child can concentrate deeply on anything at all, the capacity is there. What varies is what it will attach to, and that is mostly about the task.
what-is-executive-function-in-children:
Executive function is the mental control system: the set of processes that let somebody start something, hold on to what they are doing, stop themselves doing something else, and change approach when the first one fails. It is the machinery behind almost everything adults describe as being sensible, and it is under construction for the whole of childhood and well past it.

The three parts

Most accounts break it into three, and the split is useful because a child can be strong in one and weak in another.

  • Working memory. Holding information in mind while doing something with it. Remembering the second half of an instruction. Keeping the beginning of a sentence in mind while reading the end of it. Doing a sum without writing every step down.
  • Inhibition. Not doing the first thing that occurs to you. Not shouting the answer, not grabbing, not hitting when furious, not opening the game when the homework is out. This is the slowest to mature and the most visible when it is absent.
  • Cognitive flexibility. Switching approach when something is not working; seeing a problem from another angle; coping when a plan changes. This is what is under strain when a small change to the routine produces a large reaction.

A great deal of what gets described as attitude is a nine-year-old's inhibition doing exactly what a nine-year-old's inhibition does.

Why it matters that it develops slowly

These capacities improve steadily through childhood and continue maturing into the mid-twenties. That timeline is the single most useful thing a parent can know about it, because it reframes an enormous amount of daily friction.

A seven-year-old who cannot hold a four-part instruction, an eleven-year-old who forgets the bag every week, a fourteen-year-old who leaves an essay to the last night. None of these are character. They are a system that is not finished, being asked to perform like one that is.

This is not an argument for expecting nothing. It is an argument for scaffolding: providing from the outside what the child cannot yet provide from within, and withdrawing it gradually.

What it looks like in ordinary life

  • Getting started on something they do not want to do
  • Remembering what they went upstairs for
  • Waiting for a turn without the wait becoming unbearable
  • Stopping one activity to begin another
  • Coping when the plan changes at short notice
  • Keeping track of belongings across a day
  • Planning backwards from a deadline

Why it is worth attending to

Executive function is one of the better predictors of how children get on at school, in some studies comparable to early ability measures, and it is associated with a range of outcomes beyond academics. It is also more malleable than raw ability, which is why it is worth building deliberately.

Two cautions. Most of that evidence is correlational, so it shows association rather than proof of cause. And commercial brain-training aimed at these capacities has repeatedly produced gains on the trained exercise that do not transfer to schoolwork or daily life. What does appear to help is more ordinary: complex play, games with rules, physical activity, sleep, and adults who scaffold rather than either rescue or abandon.

The system is being built for the whole of childhood. Most of what looks like unwillingness is a capacity that has not arrived yet.
